opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that really excites me about the task-length framing is that it gives us a single, intuitive axis that's actually comparable across very different models and very different time periods. A lot of benchmarks have this problem where they're useful for a year or two, and then they saturate, and you can't really say anything about how a model from 2019 relates to a model from 2025 on the same scale. With task length, the basic idea is: we take a bunch of tasks, we measure how long it takes skilled humans to do them, and then we ask, for a given model, what's the length of task at which it succeeds, say, 50% of the time. That number turns out to be surprisingly well-behaved. When you plot it over time, you get something that looks roughly like an exponential trend, with the time horizon doubling every several months.

And I think that's significant for a couple of reasons. One is just that it's interpretable. If I tell you a model has a 70% score on some benchmark, it's not obvious what that means for the world. But if I tell you a model can reliably do tasks that take a human expert about an hour, versus tasks that take a week or a month, that maps much more directly onto questions people actually care about, like what kinds of work could be automated, or when systems might be able to do substantial chunks of AI research themselves.

The other reason is that length seems to capture something real about what's hard for these systems. Short tasks are often mostly about knowledge, knowing the right fact or the right trick. Longer tasks require things like planning, recovering from mistakes, keeping track of context, noticing when you've gone down the wrong path. Those are exactly the capabilities that matter for agency, and they've historically been where models struggle.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell it. There are real caveats. The tasks we use are mostly software and research-engineering tasks, which are relatively well-specified and have clean success criteria, so they may not be representative of messier real-world work. The human baselines are noisy. And it's an open question how well the trend extrapolates, whether it speeds up, slows down, or whether the metric itself starts to break down at longer horizons. But as a way of tracking progress in a way that's legible and forecastable, I think it's one of the more useful tools we have right now.

r001.rationale: The response defines the horizon as the human completion time of tasks a model can do, and gives 50% success as an example of the specified success probability.

r002.rationale: It describes an approximately exponential trend with doubling every several months, but does not state that the trend covers roughly the preceding five years.

r003.rationale: It presents task length as comparable across models and time periods, but does not clearly identify human completion time as a common metric for comparisons across different benchmarks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's significant about it is that it gives you a way to talk about progress that actually connects to what people care about, which is: what can these systems do in the world? A lot of benchmarks are sort of self-referential. You make a test, models get better at the test, and it's not obvious what that means for anything outside the test. Whereas if you say "this model can reliably do tasks that take a skilled human an hour, and last year it could only do tasks that took a few minutes," that's a statement about capability that a non-expert can actually reason about.

The other thing I'd say is that it captures something that per-task accuracy numbers miss, which is the ability to string together many steps without falling over. Historically, models were pretty good at individual steps and pretty bad at not making a mistake somewhere across a long sequence of them, or at noticing the mistake and recovering. So task length is kind of a proxy for coherence and error correction, and those are the things that gate whether you can delegate real work rather than just asking a question and getting an answer.

Now, I want to be careful about it, because "task length" is a somewhat slippery thing. You have to decide how long a task takes for whom, and under what conditions, and the tasks you measure with are never going to be a perfectly representative sample of real work. There's a lot of messiness in the real world that doesn't show up in a nicely scoped eval task. So I don't think it's a crisp quantity so much as a useful lens. But I do think the trend you see when you look at it that way, where the horizon seems to be growing fairly steadily over time, is one of the more informative things we have for thinking about where this is going and how fast.

r001.rationale: The response gives an example of reliably completing tasks that take a skilled human an hour, but does not define task horizon using a specified success probability.

r002.rationale: It says the task horizon has grown fairly steadily over time, without describing approximately exponential growth or specifying a roughly five-year period.

r003.rationale: The response discusses task length as a useful capability measure, but does not identify human completion time as a common metric for comparing capabilities across benchmarks.

astra-6.text:
I think it gives us a more intuitive way to understand what improving model capabilities actually means. A benchmark score going from 60 to 80 percent can be hard to interpret. But if a model goes from reliably completing tasks that take a human a few minutes to tasks that take a human several hours, that tells you something fairly concrete about the kinds of work you might be able to delegate to it.

And longer tasks often require getting a whole sequence of things right—maintaining context, noticing mistakes, recovering when an approach fails. So this measure can capture something that’s missing when we only test isolated questions.

The important caveat is that human task duration isn’t a universal measure of difficulty for an AI. It matters which tasks you’re sampling and how reliably the model needs to succeed. I’d see it as a useful lens on progress, rather than a single number that captures everything.

r003.rationale: It does not identify human task-completion time as a common metric for comparing capabilities across benchmarks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing is that it gives us a way to connect improvements in model capabilities to something we actually care about: how much work can these systems do autonomously? A benchmark score going from 60 to 70 percent can be hard to interpret. If a system goes from reliably doing tasks that take a human five minutes to tasks that take a human an hour, that’s a much more concrete change.

And task length puts pressure on a capability that’s easy to miss in short evaluations, which is maintaining reliable behavior over many steps. A model might be able to do each individual step reasonably well, but still fail at the overall task because it makes a mistake, doesn’t notice it, or gets stuck and can’t recover.

The caveat is that human completion time isn’t a universal measure of difficulty. Some long tasks are repetitive and straightforward, and some very short tasks require a lot of insight. So I’d view this as a useful axis of progress, especially for autonomous work, rather than a single number that captures everything about intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response compares tasks by human completion time, but does not define a task horizon using a specified model success probability.

r002.rationale: It does not describe an approximately exponential growth trend in task durations over the preceding five years.

r003.rationale: It contrasts task length with benchmark scores, but does not state that human task-completion time is a common metric for comparing capabilities across benchmarks.
